title: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (5 of 7)
hook: a Rajput princess who said she was already married, to Krishna
tomorrow: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (6 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Nayanars, and Kannappa the hunter, who gave his eye. Love before the rules. Your line: love as the road. Did you receive someone's clumsy love kindly? Day two hundred seventy-one.

Rajasthan, in the days of the Rajput kingdoms. The story goes that a little girl in a royal family sees a wedding procession go by and asks her mother: who will I marry? And her mother, half joking, points to a small image of Krishna and says: him. The girl takes it completely seriously. She grows up, she's married off to a prince of a powerful royal house, and she tells everyone, calmly, that she was already married. To Krishna. Her name was Mira. Her songs are still sung today.
screen: `WHO WILL I MARRY?` → `HIM, SAYS HER MOTHER.` → `ALREADY MARRIED, TO KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers Mirabai as a princess of Merta who married into the royal house of Mewar. Honest note first: we know very little about her for certain. Most of what's told comes from devotional tradition, and many of the songs sung in her name were likely composed later by others who loved her. But the Mira of those songs and stories is unforgettable. Her husband, tradition says, died young, and she refused to behave the way a royal widow was expected to. She sang and danced in the temple, in public, with wandering holy people, which scandalized her in-laws. Her refrain, in a song still widely sung, is roughly: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. Giridhar: the one who lifted the mountain. Gopal: the cowherd. Krishna. Then the famous story. Her in-laws, the tradition says, sent her a cup of poison, disguised as holy water offered to Krishna. Mira drank it, because it came as an offering to her beloved. And it didn't harm her. Another time, a snake in a basket, and when she opened it she found a garland, or an image of Krishna. Eventually she left the palace, walked to Vrindavan, Krishna's childhood country, and then to Dwarka, on the western coast, where tradition says she disappeared into Krishna's image. What Mira adds to bhakti is this: the love isn't only reverence. It can be the love of a bride, bold, personal, and willing to lose everything the world thinks matters.
screen: `A PRINCESS OF MERTA AND MEWAR.` · `MINE IS GIRIDHAR GOPAL.` · `THE CUP OF POISON.` · `FROM THE PALACE TO DWARKA.` · then, large: `LOVE AS THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask yourself what you'd keep if everything else were taken. Not things. The thing you love most, the one you'd walk out of a palace for. Maybe it's a person, maybe a faith, maybe something you've never said aloud. Breathe in, and let yourself know it. Breathe out, and let it stand plainly, without apology. If you pray, you can hold it up to God as Mira held up hers. If not, just let it be yours. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti yoga, through Mirabai: the Rajput poet-saint whose love for Krishna was the love of a bride, bold and personal. Mine is Giridhar Gopal.
Your line: love as the road. Today, do one thing you love openly that you usually hide a little, singing, dancing, praying, and let it be seen. Day two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Mirabai's bhajans are sung across North India and the diaspora, in temples, homes and concerts; many devotees know her as the model of madhurya bhava, love for Krishna as a beloved.

original.note: Hindi/Braj: Giridhar Gopal, 'the mountain-lifter, the cowherd,' Mira's name for Krishna.

trapdoor: what you thought: devotion to God is always quiet and respectful.
what it means: in Mira's bhakti, love for Krishna is a bride's love, bold and willing to lose everything.

what a scholar hears: Mira's historical life is thinly documented; the corpus of 'Mira' songs grew over centuries in Rajasthani, Braj and Gujarati, and scholars treat it as a living tradition more than one author's collected works.
